I have played this game before back in 2010, and for reasons I can't rightly remember I did not like it at the time. I don't think I spent more than hour playing. Fast forward to now,  I was looking for a 'summer game' that would not turn my computer into a space heater, and chanced upon this game, and thought: I should give this another shot. 

What I wasn't aware of when I bought it is that the game was clearly never designed to operate on modern hardware, and despite having a high-end PC, I still found that the game consumed more resources than what I had expected based on how awful the game looks by today's standards. The game was designed to operate on a single processor core, and cannot consume all of the available memory even after applying various fixes as well as third party utilities such as a 4gb patch. So the game bottlenecks the computer. As unforunate as that sounds, that alone doesn't warrant a negative review and I decided to push on despite the summer conditions. The game still runs cooler than many modern triple A titles after all, and I managed to get it running in a stable and satisfactory fashion. 

I had played Inquisition in the past, and found it enjoyable enough to warrant about 3 playthroughs. Decent as it was, it wasn't quite memorable to me and it took me forever to recognize many of the characters already present in this game. Granted, my last playthrough in Inquisition was probably about 7 years ago, but I still find it important to mention considering how much time I must have spent on that. Inquisition was just never among the RPG greats. 

So firing up the campaign and creating a character, I had an excellent first impression, and I thought I was in for a good time. The controls are clunky, but considering my past experience with BG3 and Inquisition I got the hang of it very quickly. The story itself isn't particularily original, but the game comes with a cast of strong characters that have their own personalities, traits and differe…

This is my second attempt at playing DA:O--my first was two years ago on Game Pass, and I got frustrated with constant crashes and dropped it early on. This time, I appear to have found the right balance of mods and performance settings, and I haven't had a crash yet in the first 7 hours. Knock on wood that that'll continue.

I really enjoy the setting, world-building, storytelling, and real-time with pause tactical combat of DA:O. I am not too far into the game, but I have now played through two of the different origin starting points if you combine my two starts, and I am really impressed by both of them--they are completely different, satisfying, bite-sized little narrative games in their own right. I am excited to actually finish the game this time!

That said, I am disgusted that BioWare/EA are actively selling a game that requires mod support for basic functionality. Before you sink your teeth into this game, you essentially have to spend the first few hours of your playthrough on the Steam forums and NexusMods trying to make sure that you won't have a bad time once you hit "Play." This game is considered a classic of the genre, and there's no way that sales volume is low enough that they couldn't make some basic fixes to the port so that it works properly on PC hardware. There's a mod that allows the game to use more RAM. Is that not just an obvious fix for the supposed "ultimate" edition to include out of the box?

The game itself holds up very well in 2026, but its technical state is in shambles. Buyer beware.

Got this on sale. The game itself is one of my favorites of all time. However, this port is terrible, constantly crashing despite my computer not having terrible specs.

Not worth the time unless you want to spend hours trying to tweak settings and figuring out how to get mods to work in order just to run the game.

I'm a big fan of the Dragon Age series, played it to death on console, but I cannot recommend Origins on Steam. It simply does not play well with modern computers. The game crashed constantly until I changed specific settings based on another player's advice (frame buffer effects off, vsync off, and texture details low/medium, if anyone's wondering). Screenshots still cause a crash no matter what, unfortunately. And there are other snags beyond that: the worst of which is a strange bug that causes all characters to get stuck whenever they reach the top of a staircase. This happens on every single set of stairs or weird bump in the terrain, and the only way I've found to fix it is to jiggle the camera. It's not good, man.

If anyone is looking to get into the series, I'd recommend Inquisition or maybe Veilguard. Origins is really only an option if you're a diehard fan looking to get into the weeds with the lore. Even then, it's hardly worth the headache, even if you catch one of the sales where it's like $3.

Game is not designed to run on modern systems and will crash as soon as you try loading a save. I've tried the 4GB patch, I've tried the unencrypted exe, I've tried setting it to only use 1 core, I've tried DXsetup, I've tried blocking onedrive, I've tried setting my graphics to Medium, I've tried modifying the launcher's XML, I've running in compatibility mode, I've tried everything suggested by ever guide but buying it on the EA App or on GOG because quite frankly, no game is worth this much effort.

From what ive seen so far the gameplay, characters, etc are great, although just be prepared for a ton of crashing, Youll have to lower graphics, install mods and more to stop the game from dying on you.

Dragon Age: Origins - Ultimate Edition is an absolute masterpiece and widely considered one of the greatest dark fantasy RPGs ever made. It delivers a massive, tactical epic with unforgettable choices, though modern PC players will need a couple of quick mod fixes to keep it running smoothly today.
Here is what makes it incredible:
True Roleplaying: Your chosen origin story (like a Noble Dwarf or Elven Mage) completely changes how the world reacts to you throughout the entire game.
Masterful Companions: From Morrigan to Alistair, the party dynamics and romance options set the gold standard for RPG writing.
Deep Tactical Combat: It plays like a classic real-time-with-pause cRPG, letting you program intricate battle tactics for your companion AI.
Massive Value: The Ultimate Edition packs in the massive Awakening expansion and all 8 DLCs, offering over 100 hours of peak storytelling.
Essential Modding: The community has fixed the game's infamous modern PC memory leaks. Dragging community patches into your override folder prevents crashes and unlocks beautiful HD textures.
It is an unforgettable, gritty adventure that every RPG fan needs to experience at least once.

Maybe wait for a sale if you're not sure (it gets very cheap occasionally), but this is a classic for a reason.

The combat is a little strange by modern standards, but good - it's somewhere in-between a typical modern RPG and a MOBA.  It'll run on a potato - given the age of the game, it's not a shock that it'll do OK on modern integrated graphics (!), but it still looks surprisingly decent.  The worldbuilding and immersion is just [chef's kiss] - twenty seconds and two dialog choices in and I had a feel for the character I was playing; and most of the ongoing political, moral, and personal quandaries add layers to the world and main character.  The writing isn't flawless, but it works with complicated social and political issues without pretending they don't exist or being preaching and condescending.

It's crashing semi-regularly (memory leak?), but that's not a huge deal if you save frequently, and scaling on large monitors isn't great.  Possibly mods help with one or both of those?

TLDR; despite the limitations and age, I'd put it on the shortlist of 'games you really ought to play at some point'.   If you like RPGs, do yourself a favor and pick it up next time it's on sale.  Or if you're bored, not to price sensitive, and like the old Bioware stuff (in some ways it very much reminds me of ME1), go ahead and pay list, you'll still get your money's worth.

This game was one of the first RPGs in a long time that actually got me to role-play my character (City Elf Warrior). The writing in this game is superb, the origin system is immaculate, and the friends met along the way will be etched in my memories forever. I love Alistair, and Leliana, and Morrigan, and I appreciate the fact that my characters relationship to each of them felt genuine and nonreplicable - that’s how you know the story telling is perfect. The only thing I complaint  is that there are so  many characters that I couldn’t see all their stories and really connect with them (I’m looking at you Sten) all in one run… I guess that adds to the replay value though!

Though there are some issues with the game running on PC, glitches and crashes and what not, these are all things that come simply with the age of the game. The part of this game that aged the best was the story, this is a story that I dreamed of when I first started playing RPGs as a child. I wanted a game that your actions actually mattered. Your decisions reflect greatly on your character, and not only that you are someone that is still talked about like an old legend within the other games. You aren't faceless or simply someone who happened to make the change before anyone else could. You ARE that person and you always will be.

citations.review_text:
Maybe wait for a sale if you're not sure (it gets very cheap occasionally), but this is a classic for a reason.

The combat is a little strange by modern standards, but good - it's somewhere in-between a typical modern RPG and a MOBA.  It'll run on a potato - given the age of the game, it's not a shock that it'll do OK on modern integrated graphics (!), but it still looks surprisingly decent.  The worldbuilding and immersion is just [chef's kiss] - twenty seconds and two dialog choices in and I had a feel for the character I was playing; and most of the ongoing political, moral, and personal quandaries add layers to the world and main character.  The writing isn't flawless, but it works with complicated social and political issues without pretending they don't exist or being preaching and condescending.

It's crashing semi-regularly (memory leak?), but that's not a huge deal if you save frequently, and scaling on large monitors isn't great.  Possibly mods help with one or both of those?

TLDR; despite the limitations and age, I'd put it on the shortlist of 'games you really ought to play at some point'.   If you like RPGs, do yourself a favor and pick it up next time it's on sale.  Or if you're bored, not to price sensitive, and like the old Bioware stuff (in some ways it very much reminds me of ME1), go ahead and pay list, you'll still get your money's worth.
Love this game so much. The companions are memorable and interesting, the combat is dynamic, the storyline and lore is grand. Just such a great experience, and the ending cutscene was really awesome.

Haven't played this game since launch, and I didn't fully appreciate it back then, but this time I totally get why everyone's still praising DA:O to this day.
This game is big, ambitious, and feels very confident in its quality, and for good reason.
Pretty much every game mechanic you would expect from a Bioware game from the late 00s and early 10s is here (except for a morality system I guess, but I didn't miss it), but it's all better and deeper, with more variety.
I'm usually not into tactical combat systems, and it was miserable at first, as this game is not easy. But by the mid-game, once I got used to it, it became super fun to explore and find more and more combinations and tactics that work better against different types of enemies.

The central plot will feel familiar to any Bioware fan, hitting many familiar beats, and it feels corny at times. I also found some of the dialogue to be a bit too edgy, like bringing up very explicit themes without properly addressing them. It works for the atmosphere the game is going for, as the world of DA: Origins is supposed to be bleak and depressing. I just wish some of this "darkness" was handled with a bit more finesse.
But overall, the story totally works because of the amazing cast of characters in your party and the deep lore of this miserable, dark world - so again, Bioware at its best.

Dragon Age: Origins is one of those games that feels almost impossible to make today. I bought it when I was younger, a few years after it had originally released, and I still remember the guy at the store telling me: “This game is wonderful. It will change the way you look at every other game.”

He was right. Playing it again after all these years, I’m amazed by how much of its brilliance has remained intact.

Its greatest strength, in my opinion, is its realism and brutality. Origins understands that you don’t need spectacular magic, colorful worlds, or constant epic moments to make a fantasy world immersive. Sometimes, all you need is crudeness. The world feels dirty, harsh, morally complicated, and believable. Magic exists, but it’s never allowed to overshadow the grounded feeling of the setting. This is something I genuinely hope more games start doing again, because there’s something incredibly immersive about a world that isn’t afraid to be ugly, cruel, and uncomfortable.

The choices are another huge strength. They have real consequences, and being “good” isn’t always the best option. Sometimes there simply isn’t a right answer, only different kinds of consequences.

The companions are also incredibly well written (SPOILERS). Alistair and Leliana are particularly deep characters, with personal stories and development that make them feel like actual people rather than simple party members. And then there’s Morrigan, who might be one of the most fascinating characters in the entire series. Her worldview, her cynicism, and the way her character gradually develops make every interaction with her memorable.

The combat is strategic, but much deeper than it initially appears. Character progression feels natural, and the game maintains a fantastic rhythm between narrative progression, exploration, character development, and combat.

A timeless masterpiece that shows how far the gaming industry has fallen.

Despite being an older game Dragon Age Origins provided me with an incredible experience. Playing this classic today really opens your eyes to a harsh reality showing you exactly how much the gaming industry has declined and how modern RPGs lost their true soul.

The best part of this game is the writing and the characters. From that very first encounter with Morrigan to meeting Leliana and the rest of the companions you immediately realize that every character carries real weight in this world. Their backstories are so well crafted that you genuinely care about seeing how they will confront their personal enemies and struggles. You aren't just traveling with NPCs you are traveling with deeply written companions.

The gameplay is solid for a classic RPG. The mechanics are deep understandable and not frustratingly complicated. The leveling and character progression system is perfectly balanced and satisfying. If you compare this older title to the recent release The Veilguard Origins completely outshines it in every core aspect like writing character depth and player choice. The only area where The Veilguard actually wins is the modern fluidity of its action combat but everywhere else it’s a massive step backward for the franchise.

The only downside is the graphics which naturally look outdated by today's standards. But the story is so gripping and the characters are so well written that this visual flaw didn't negatively impact my experience at all. I was so deeply immersed in the world that I completely forgot about the graphics and simply enjoyed every single moment.

It is an unforgettable experience and a must-play for anyone who wants to see what a true RPG looks like.

Rating: 9/10

The combat in here is shallow and hardly works. Have to toggle your follows to fight pretty damn often. And then constantly seeing the *miss *miss *miss and low scores. Crafting is another issue. The stores would be nice to have a refresh option so you can build up some ingredients to make potions or poisons. 

Back in the day, this game is good. It was a total beast of an title.

I've tried so hard to like this game, but I think it's a classic case of "you just had to be there". I don't enjoy many of its design choices. The combat is sluggish, character talents and skills aren't too exciting and you'll be micromanaging most things because the Tactics system is janky. I've never felt so bored by combat in a RPG before.

The game is also not open world. Which, fine. They can't all be. But it makes the game world feel like a collection of random areas than a cohesive world. Worse, you travel from each distinct area by selecting markers on a map. Once done you're left watching your party slowly travel to the marker you've selected. There are occasional random encounters where you actually do things, but once you're far enough into the story they mostly stop. So you just sit and wait for your party to travel. Riveting stuff. An actual loading screen would've been preferable.

I also can't for the life of me find enjoyment in the writing. This game wasn't breaking ground when it released, and time hasn't been kind to it. It's relatively inoffensive dark fantasy that marketed as being morally complicated, but the vast majority of choices you make are between textbook versions of good and evil. So boring.

Needless to say, I've had a pretty bad time with this but also have a feeling the game would benefit greatly from a remake.

Dragon Age: Origins is not just my favorite game in the Dragon Age franchise — it’s one of my favorite RPGs ever made. This is where the franchise started, and even after all these years, it still stands as the gold standard for player choice and storytelling.

What makes this game so special is how much freedom it gives you to truly shape your character. You can be a noble hero, a ruthless monster, a sarcastic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, or somewhere in between. The game doesn’t force you into being “good” or “evil” — it genuinely lets you roleplay however you want, and the world reacts to your choices in meaningful ways. So many RPGs claim your decisions matter, but Dragon Age: Origins actually delivers on that promise.

The origin stories alone are incredible and immediately make your character feel personal and connected to the world. Then the story just keeps getting better from there. The political conflicts, the companions, the betrayals, the emotional moments — it all feels so well written and memorable. The companions especially are some of the best in gaming, with conversations and relationships that still stick with me years later.

You can tell the developers poured their hearts into this game. Every choice feels intentional, every companion has depth, and every playthrough can feel completely different depending on the type of character you create.

Dragon Age: Origins is a masterpiece of RPG design and storytelling. Games like this are the reason people fall in love with the genre.

Incredibly fun if you're into old school RPG games. Real time pause & decide, then unpause and watch it play out, rinse and repeat. On easier difficulties you can just play your own character in real time like WoW or other MMO's, but on higher difficulties you really gotta make use of the pausing and team coordination. Very fun if you can get the game to work on your newer machine!

I guess my only complaint is that it has a tendency to crash at the most inconvenient times. Remember to save often
Other than that i have only good things to say about it, everything you'd want in an RPG is here
